strengths: Originality: 3DGSim presents a novel and technically interesting integration of feed-forward multi-view reconstruction, latent 3D Gaussians, space-filling-curve serialization, and a temporally merged Point Transformer. Reusing attention blocks across merged timesteps is a useful architectural idea.

Significance: End-to-end learning of an editable 3D simulator from calibrated RGB observations is an important problem, and the unified reconstruction-dynamics-rendering pipeline could become a valuable research baseline.

Soundness: The experiments cover three qualitatively different synthetic regimes—rigid bodies, elastoplastic objects, and cloth—and report long autoregressive rollouts, novel-view metrics, speed, memory use, and several hyperparameter ablations.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript describes the loss, architecture dimensions, camera sampling, dataset sizes, optimizer, training duration, and major hyperparameters in useful detail. It also promises release of code and newly generated datasets.

The qualitative scene edits, multi-object compositions, learned boundary conditions, and appearance changes such as shadows are promising demonstrations of capabilities beyond straightforward next-frame rendering.

Limitations and ethics: The paper honestly acknowledges reliance on multi-view data, incomplete occlusion handling, lack of action conditioning, and the absence of real-world validation. The synthetic datasets raise no evident human-subject or privacy concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of learning physically realistic and generalizable simulation is not adequately validated. Evaluation uses only image-space PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; there are no 3D trajectory, contact, rigidity, deformation, constraint-violation, energy, or stability measurements. Image metrics conflate inverse-rendering quality with dynamics and can reward blurry or nearly static predictions.

The only quantitative baseline is Cosmos, which the authors themselves acknowledge is not directly comparable: it is a pretrained single-view video generator with different conditioning, representation, and inputs. Missing baselines include copy/constant-velocity prediction, a GNN or kNN dynamics model, plain PTv3, and comparable reconstruction-plus-dynamics systems. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that the proposed transformer or temporal-merging design is responsible for the gains.

The strongest generalization claims are supported almost entirely by selected qualitative examples. The random 12% trajectory split retains the same small collection of object identities and simulation domains across training and test. Unseen-object, multi-body, ground-removal, and 180-step claims lack quantitative metrics, sample counts, failure rates, or clearly defined held-out splits.

The component ablations are insufficient. There is no controlled removal of temporal merging, learned view-independent feature transformation, joint encoder training, invariant/dynamic decomposition, or SFC serialization, nor a comparison against kNN attention. Temporal-merger variants are mostly trained for 80k steps while the selected model is trained for 120k, confounding that table.

Statistical reporting is unclear: the meaning of the reported ± values is unspecified, results apparently come from single training runs, and neither seed variation nor uncertainty over training is reported. This matters for a five-day training procedure and for several relatively close comparisons.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite substantial implementation detail. The manuscript says code and data “will” be released but supplies no verifiable artifact, while particle counts, explicit feature size nf, masking details, rollout mechanics, evaluation aggregation, data-generation parameters, and exact split construction are not fully specified.

The framing overstates the input assumptions: the system requires calibrated multi-view cameras through projection matrices and usually uses foreground/static segmentation masks, so describing it simply as operating from raw RGB video is potentially misleading. The supplementary ablation shows that very sparse camera setups fail.

Significance is presently limited by evaluation only on clean synthetic data generated from a few objects and highly uniform scenes. No real-video result tests reconstruction errors, imperfect calibration, occlusion, lighting changes, or domain shift, all of which are central to the stated robotics motivation.

Presentation needs polishing. Page 1 has overlapping figure/caption and body text, the main comparison table is extremely small, some figure/table references are inconsistent, and numerous grammatical or typographical errors and underspecified notation make the method harder to verify.

Overall, the architecture is promising, but unsupported physical-generalization claims and the lack of meaningful comparable baselines are material evidential gaps. A revision with dynamics-specific quantitative evaluation, rigorous OOD splits, controlled component baselines, multiple seeds, and an accessible release would be needed before others could reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper presents a potentially useful end-to-end combination of multi-view RGB reconstruction, latent particle dynamics, temporal point-cloud processing, and Gaussian-splat rendering. The temporal serialization/merging mechanism is a sensible extension of PTv3 for multi-frame inputs.

Soundness: The experiments span rigid, elastic, and cloth simulations, and the trajectory plots report degradation over long rollouts rather than only one-step prediction. The latent-versus-explicit, rollout-length, camera-count, masking, grid-resolution, and temporal-merging studies provide some useful diagnostic evidence.

Presentation: The pipeline is generally understandable, with helpful architecture diagrams, equations, qualitative rollouts, and a candid limitations section acknowledging reliance on multi-view synthetic data, incomplete occlusion handling, lack of action conditioning, and absence of real-world validation.

Reproducibility/ethics: Dataset sizes, camera counts, optimizer, training duration, principal architecture dimensions, and hardware are reported. The experiments use synthetic data and raise no evident material safety or human-subject concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claims of learning physical interactions, robust physical generalization, and counterfactual reasoning are not supported by the evaluation. The reported metrics—PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS—measure rendered appearance, not trajectory accuracy, conservation behavior, collision correctness, deformation accuracy, or other physical quantities. A model can score well by predicting plausible images without learning correct dynamics.

Soundness: The only quantitative comparator is Cosmos, a pretrained single-view video generator that the authors explicitly acknowledge is not directly comparable to their multi-view system. No particle simulator, neural rendering-dynamics method, reconstruction-plus-dynamics pipeline, or simple persistence/constant-velocity baseline is evaluated. The absence of public implementations for selected prior work does not justify omitting implementable or component-level baselines, so the claimed advantage of the proposed design cannot be established.

Soundness: The strongest generalization claims rely almost entirely on qualitative demonstrations without ground truth or quantitative tests. Randomly holding out 12% of trajectories appears to leave the same six objects and simulation families in training and testing. The multi-body examples duplicate objects even though training contains only object-ground collisions, but no reference trajectories or physical metrics are supplied; Figure 10 even describes objects being pushed through the table and color changes/falling particles, which is evidence of failure rather than correct interaction modeling.

Soundness/originality: Most components are inherited from MVSplat, PTv3, FiLM, and standard Gaussian splatting. The principal new mechanism—bit-shift temporal merging—receives an ablation in which the selected model is trained for 120k steps while most alternatives are trained for 80k, confounding architectural benefit with optimization time. There is also no controlled comparison against ordinary spatiotemporal attention, explicit correspondence, kNN/GNN processing, or PTv3 without the complete set of proposed changes.

Significance: The empirical scope is narrow: all results come from three synthetic, highly controlled falling-object settings, with fixed simulator families, backgrounds, cameras, and a small object collection. There is no real video, robot action, external force input, material transfer test, cross-simulator test, or evaluation on substantially different scene geometry. Consequently, the paper does not demonstrate the robotics relevance or data-rich scalability emphasized in its motivation.

Reproducibility: The manuscript promises a future code and dataset release but provides no accessible artifact in the paper. Important information is missing or ambiguous, including complete simulator/material parameters, train/test generation details, random seeds and number of runs, precise uncertainty computation, preprocessing and masks, super-resolution usage, and full evaluation protocol. Some reporting is internally inconsistent—for example, the camera-setup discussion attributes PSNR 33.15 to the 3-of-6 setting although its table reports 31.60, and the modality prose reports 32.27 where the table reports 31.98.

Presentation: The paper repeatedly overinterprets visual results, using phrases such as “adapts seamlessly,” “correctly captures realistic multi-body dynamics,” and “robust understanding of physics” without corresponding measurements. Several technical definitions also need correction or clarification, including allocating log2(T) bits without specifying rounding or restricting T, ambiguous indexing/normalization in the loss, and incomplete justification for calling learned camera-conditioned features canonical or view-independent.

Limitations/ethics: The limitations discussion is welcome but omits decisive evaluation limitations: appearance metrics are not physics metrics, the baseline is mismatched, the test split may not assess object-level generalization, and qualitative scene edits have no ground truth. Dataset licensing and provenance for the selected GSO assets should also be stated. These are not major ethical risks, but they affect responsible release and reproducibility.

strengths: Soundness: The proposed pipeline is technically coherent: it jointly connects multi-view reconstruction, view-independent particle features, temporally serialized Point Transformer dynamics, and differentiable Gaussian-splat rendering. Experiments cover rigid, elastic, and cloth dynamics, and the rollout-length and temporal-merging ablations support several design choices.

Significance: Learning an editable 3D simulator directly from RGB videos, without depth or ground-truth particle trajectories, addresses an important problem. The reported 12–42 FPS simulation rates and sub-20 GB inference memory suggest practical promise.

Originality: The combination of MVSplat, temporally augmented space-filling-curve serialization, hierarchical temporal merging, and 3D Gaussian decoding is a novel and useful synthesis. In particular, temporal merging provides an interesting alternative to explicit correspondence or separately parameterized per-step modules.

Presentation: The paper clearly motivates the problem, explains the architecture with helpful diagrams, and includes extensive qualitative rollout visualizations. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on multi-view data, occlusion issues, absence of action conditioning, and lack of real-world validation.

Reproducibility: The manuscript provides substantial architectural and training detail, including feature dimensions, block depths, attention configuration, grid size, loss weights, rollout lengths, optimizer, compute, and training duration. The promised release of code and datasets would establish a useful benchmark.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evaluation primarily measures rendered-image similarity (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS), not physical correctness. There are no trajectory, pose, deformation, contact, energy, or constraint-violation metrics. Consequently, strong claims that the model understands physics or correctly captures multi-body dynamics are not established by the presented evidence.

Evaluation: Cosmos is an imperfect and relatively weak comparator because it is a single-view pretrained video generator, whereas 3DGSim receives calibrated multi-view observations and explicitly reconstructs 3D. The absence of adapted particle-simulator, dynamic-3D-reconstruction, simple persistence/constant-velocity, or oracle-state baselines makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of the dynamics model.

Generalization: The random 12% trajectory split appears to retain the same object identities and simulator distributions across training and testing. The more ambitious claims involving unseen objects, ground removal, changed height, and multiple bodies rely almost entirely on qualitative examples without ground truth or quantitative evaluation; some examples also exhibit failure behavior such as objects passing through the table.

Ablations: Important components are not cleanly isolated. The paper does not compare the proposed transformer against a matched kNN/GNN dynamics model, standard PTv3 without temporal merging, or alternative temporal aggregation under comparable compute. Reported temporal-merger variants are also trained for 80k steps while the selected model uses 120k, confounding architecture and training budget.

Reproducibility and presentation: The paper promises rather than demonstrates code and dataset availability, and dataset-generation details such as initial-condition distributions, camera layouts, object splits, preprocessing, mask construction, and random seeds are incomplete. Error bars are not clearly defined, results from multiple training seeds are absent, and a few table/text inconsistencies and typographical issues reduce precision.

Scope and ethics: All evidence is synthetic, despite motivation centered on real robotics, and the method requires calibrated multi-view cameras and several days on an H100. The paper honestly identifies the missing real-world validation, which should not itself be penalized, but deployment-oriented claims should be moderated. No major ethical concern is apparent, although dataset licensing and the risks of relying on visually plausible but physically inaccurate predictions in robotics deserve brief discussion.

strengths: Soundness: The end-to-end formulation is technically coherent: multi-view RGB observations are converted into latent 3D particles, evolved with a Point Transformer, and decoded through differentiable Gaussian splatting. The invariant/dynamic feature split and causal rollout objective are sensible design choices.

Originality: Adapting PTv3 to temporal point sets through serialized temporal codes, learned temporal embeddings, and hierarchical temporal merging is a novel and potentially useful contribution. The combination with jointly trained inverse rendering distinguishes the work from methods that assume ground-truth particles or use fixed analytical simulators.

The ablations identify several important dependencies. On the elastic benchmark, removing temporal encoding/merging reduces future PSNR from 33.15 to 18.19, shortening training rollouts to two steps reduces it to 26.43, and replacing latent features with explicit Gaussian parameters reduces it to 29.69.

Significance: Learning visually grounded 3D dynamics without ground-truth geometry, particle correspondence, or material labels is an important problem. Explicit scene editing and approximately real-time rollout are promising for robotics and interactive simulation.

Presentation: The main pipeline, architecture, training setup, and broad experimental conclusions are generally understandable. The supplement provides useful implementation details, extensive qualitative sequences, ablations, failure analysis, and inference speed and memory figures.

The paper acknowledges meaningful limitations, including dependence on multi-view observations, difficulty creating or destroying particles, sensitivity to the number of input views and frames, occlusion handling, and autoregressive degradation in real-world rollouts.
weaknesses: Soundness: The strongest claims—learning underlying physical laws, realistic multi-body interactions, spatial causality, and robust out-of-distribution physics—are supported primarily by selected images. No quantitative physical-state evaluation is provided for conservation, penetration, contact timing, rigidity, deformation, trajectory error, or constraint satisfaction, even though the synthetic generators make such measurements possible. Image metrics conflate rendering quality with dynamics and cannot establish these physical claims.

The comparative evaluation is insufficient for the breadth of the claims. The principal learned baseline is a 2D video model with a fundamentally different input/output structure. Spring-Gaus is evaluated on only three test trajectories per object, optimizes and tests on the same trajectory, and receives privileged masks and ground height. Relevant particle-dynamics approaches are omitted because adaptation is difficult, leaving the claimed state-of-the-art advantage weakly substantiated.

Generalization is not rigorously isolated. The random trajectory split appears to retain the same small set of object identities across training and test, while ground removal and multi-object composition are only qualitative. There is no object-held-out, material-held-out, camera-held-out, or statistically aggregated intervention benchmark. Consequently, the results do not distinguish transferable physics from interpolation over fixed assets and simulator parameters.

The real-world evidence is preliminary and does not validate the main raw-RGB formulation directly: it replaces MVSplat with a pretrained DepthAnything3 encoder and introduces 3D hand keypoints as action conditioning. The dataset has only 64 trajectories, the train/test protocol is unspecified, and the sole quantitative comparator is a constant-frame baseline. The displayed failure case also shows substantial fading and loss of interaction after roughly four seconds.

Several experimental details and inconsistencies hinder reproducibility. The promised code and dataset release is not accessible from the manuscript; simulator material parameters, initial-condition distributions, camera calibration and placement, random seeds, exact split construction, preprocessing and super-resolution procedures, and complete Cosmos fine-tuning settings are missing. Training one model for about six days on an H100 also makes replication costly.

The mathematical specification needs correction or clarification. Equation 9 divides the reconstruction sum by T while summing from 0 through T, does not normalize the future weighted sum, and uses ambiguous time indexing. The stated Gaussian covariance parameterization is also imprecise for rotations and scales. Such issues make an exact independent implementation harder.

Presentation contains overstatements and internal inconsistencies. For example, particle penetration and color shifting are described as evidence of a realistic cumulative-weight effect rather than potentially serious artifacts; the text claims emergent understanding of lighting and physics from shadows; object names and some reported configurations differ across sections; and the discussion contains multiple typographical errors.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations discussion is welcome but does not sufficiently qualify the central physics-generalization claims or discuss failure consequences in robotics. The impact statement is boilerplate, and the paper does not address consent, privacy, or licensing considerations associated with the real-world hand-object dataset and scanned assets, although no immediate severe ethical issue is evident.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent end-to-end system combining multi-view inverse rendering, latent 3D particles, transformer-based dynamics, and Gaussian-splat rendering. Learning this pipeline using only image reconstruction supervision is technically ambitious and potentially useful.

The temporal encoding/merging extension to PTv3 is a plausible systems contribution. Ablations show substantial degradation without temporal merging and useful effects from longer rollout training, latent rather than explicit Gaussian features, and longer input histories.

The experiments cover rigid, elastic, and cloth dynamics, include long autoregressive rollouts, and provide extensive qualitative visualizations. The preliminary HO-Cap experiment usefully explores a real-world, action-conditioned setting rather than restricting the paper entirely to synthetic data.

The manuscript is generally understandable and acknowledges several genuine limitations, including dependence on multi-view input, inability to create or destroy particles, occlusion handling, limited real-world data, and long-horizon drift. The low apparent ethical risk of the synthetic experiments is also favorable.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support the central claims of learning broadly valid physical dynamics. Evaluation relies almost entirely on image-space PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD, which conflate reconstruction, appearance, lighting, and motion. Because the synthetic data provide simulator states, the paper could evaluate center-of-mass trajectories, rotations, deformation, contacts, penetration, energy behavior, or depth/geometry without requiring particle correspondence. The appendix's non-correspondence argument does not justify omitting all geometry- and physics-sensitive metrics.

The strongest generalization claims—ground removal, unseen objects, and multi-object collision behavior—are based on a few qualitative examples without ground truth, aggregate metrics, or failure rates. Statements such as learning generalized physical laws, accurately capturing multi-body interactions, and demonstrating a holistic understanding of lighting, geometry, and physics are therefore substantially overstated. Some shown particle penetration and color shifting could equally indicate failure rather than an emergent weight effect.

The baseline evaluation is not sufficiently controlled. Cosmos receives a single-view video interface whereas 3DGSim receives calibrated multi-view observations and an explicit editable 3D state. Spring-Gaus has a materially different per-scene optimization setting and is unavailable for cloth. No competitive learned 3D dynamics baseline is implemented, and simple controls such as reconstruction-only extrapolation, optical-flow/trajectory predictors, rigid-transform fitting, or oracle-state dynamics are absent. Consequently, the results do not isolate the benefit of the proposed dynamics architecture.

The test split holds out trajectories but apparently reuses the same small collection of object identities and simulation regimes during training and testing. This establishes interpolation over initial conditions more than broad material or object generalization. There are no held-out-material, held-out-object, altered-gravity, altered-friction, or systematically varied collision tests.

The real-world study is too preliminary to substantiate practical applicability: it uses only 64 trajectories, replaces the paper's principal MVSplat encoder with a large pretrained DepthAnything3 model, supplies future hand keypoints as action conditioning, and compares quantitatively only with a constant-frame baseline. The paper reports characteristic hand fading and interaction failure after roughly four seconds but still emphasizes successful 120-step simulation.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Most of the framework is a composition of MVSplat, PTv3, and Gaussian splatting; the main architectural novelty is temporal serialization/merging. The manuscript does not compare this mechanism against straightforward full spatiotemporal attention, correspondence-based temporal fusion, or similarly parameterized alternatives, so its specific technical advantage remains unclear.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the claimed open-source release: the manuscript shows a blank project-page reference, provides limited dataset-generation and split details, omits seed-level results and uncertainty methodology, and leaves some architectural/training choices underspecified. Training takes about six days per model on an H100, making the extensive ablations costly to reproduce. There are also technical and editorial imprecisions, including inconsistent metric/configuration descriptions and several malformed sentences.

The limitations discussion is welcome but omits the most consequential limitation: image fidelity is not evidence of physical correctness. It also does not discuss compute/energy costs or the consent, privacy, and licensing status relevant to the real-world human-hand dataset and pretrained models. These are not necessarily fatal ethical issues, but appropriate documentation is missing.

strengths: Originality: 3DGSim offers a novel and coherent integration of multi-view inverse rendering, latent 3D Gaussian particles, and a transformer-only dynamics model. The temporal encoding and hierarchical merging extension to PTv3 is technically interesting and avoids explicit kNN graph construction.

Significance: Learning an editable, spatially grounded simulator directly from RGB video is an important problem for robotics and embodied intelligence. The demonstrated coverage of rigid, elastoplastic, cloth, and preliminary real-world manipulation dynamics makes the direction broadly useful.

Soundness: The main design choices receive informative ablations. On the elastic benchmark, removing temporal encoding/merging causes a large PSNR drop (33.15 to 18.19), while shorter training rollouts and explicit Gaussian features also perform substantially worse. Tests of camera count, masks, grid resolution, and temporal-merging schedules add useful diagnostic evidence.

The model generally improves future-frame PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over the fine-tuned Cosmos baseline across the three synthetic regimes; it also compares favorably with Spring-Gaus where that method is applicable. Long rollouts and editable 3D states are compelling qualitative advantages.

Presentation is generally clear and visually effective. The architecture, state decomposition, temporal serialization, training objective, datasets, and major ablations are explained in sufficient detail to understand the method.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by extensive architectural and optimization settings, dataset sizes, camera configurations, compute requirements, and supplementary ablations. The promised release of code and datasets would further increase the work's value.

The paper candidly discusses meaningful limitations, including dependence on multi-view observations, inability to create or destroy particles, degradation from autoregressive error accumulation, weak performance with very sparse cameras, and the preliminary nature of the real-world study.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning physically correct dynamics is supported mainly by image-space fidelity. PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD conflate inverse-rendering quality, appearance prediction, and physical accuracy; they cannot establish correct trajectories, contacts, rigidity, conservation behavior, or material response. The explanation that learned particles do not correspond to simulator particles is reasonable, but object-level pose, silhouettes, contact timing, penetration, or registered surface metrics could still provide more direct physical validation.

The baseline suite is limited and not fully commensurate. Cosmos is a single-view 2D video model, while Spring-Gaus receives privileged inputs, optimizes on the test trajectory, and is evaluated on only three trajectories per object. Several closely related learned 3D simulators are omitted because code or data are unavailable. Consequently, the evidence does not firmly establish superiority over the strongest relevant 3D alternatives.

The strongest out-of-distribution claims—ground removal, changed height, and multi-object interaction after single-object training—are almost entirely qualitative. There is no systematic test set, quantitative collision or penetration analysis, or comparison against strong 3D baselines for these interventions. Assertions such as a robust grasp of underlying dynamics, realistic cumulative weight, and holistic understanding of lighting, geometry, and physics are stronger than the presented evidence warrants.

Evaluation holds out trajectories but apparently retains the same object families and simulation generators across training and testing. Generalization to unseen geometries, materials, physical parameters, camera layouts, backgrounds, and simulator domains is therefore insufficiently characterized.

The real-world experiment changes the inverse renderer to pretrained DepthAnything3, uses sparse 3D hand keypoints as action conditioning, supervises only among context cameras, and compares quantitatively only with a constant-frame baseline. These results are promising but do not yet validate the principal passive RGB-only setup in realistic conditions.

The final synthetic models use foreground/static-region masks and calibrated multi-view cameras, so the headline phrasing of learning directly from raw RGB videos understates important supervision and setup assumptions. Although the no-mask ablation is encouraging, it is limited to the elastic dataset.

Reported uncertainties appear to summarize trajectory variation rather than independent training runs, and no seed-level variance or significance analysis is provided. Some conclusions are also metric-dependent: the four-frame model improves PSNR, but the two-frame model has better FVD on elastic and rigid data.

Reproducibility remains conditional on the promised code and dataset release; the manuscript provides no accessible project URL, and several dataset-generation, preprocessing, masking, evaluation, and per-experiment training details would be difficult to reconstruct exactly. Six days of H100 training per model also creates a substantial reproduction burden.

The impact statement is perfunctory. A learned simulator intended for robotics can fail under distribution shift or produce visually plausible but physically unsafe predictions; these deployment risks, dataset licensing, compute cost, and possible misuse of video-derived human-interaction data deserve more explicit treatment. No immediate disqualifying ethical concern is evident.
